sm: The host frames the central question of the episode: was Jensen Huang's companion, Alice Huang, a Chinese spy? He says there are two stories, the sex scandal that grabs public attention and the underlying story about chips reaching China. He recalls the New York Times report of November 8th, which said Nvidia opened an investigation into Huang's relationship with a woman US intelligence had determined was a Chinese spy.

The White House now says there is no evidence she was a spy. Attorney General Todd Blanche says the administration cannot operate off anonymous newspaper sourcing, and President Trump says he does not believe it about Jensen, though he calls it a different matter if chips were passed on to China. The host then turns to journalists upset that the story did not produce the outcome they wanted, and argues their job is to report accurately, not to achieve results. He closes by quoting Mike Solana, who says this is either one of the biggest Times blunders ever or a government cover-up.

Nvidia employees cheered Huang's return, and the share price jumped about 30 percent. Huang apologized to staff for putting them through it and promised to be a better CEO the second time around. The host cites the Wall Street Journal on how Nvidia has acted as a central bank to the AI boom, with investments and financing backstops worth well over a hundred billion dollars, and shares had fallen almost 28 percent after his resignation.

He notes that tech investors back Huang partly for his support of open source AI, quoting David Friedberg. Palmer Luckey says China wanted Huang out, so he wanted him back, though he disagrees with Huang on exporting chips to China. The host says the real scandal is Nvidia's relationship with China and the Commerce Department, not the affair. He describes Trump tying himself to Huang, posting a meme of Huang as Trump holding a red bra, and saying Huang made a mistake by stepping down because sex sells better than stocks.

Trump says on CNBC that he and Vice President Vance dealt with the board, and that the board's national security question was answered with no problem. The Wall Street Journal reports that Vance worked through the weekend to persuade the board, and that Trump and Vance saw Huang as a counterweight to closed source AI firms and as the best source of leverage over chip exports. The host says the White House version is that the Times botched the story and tried to take out a powerful CEO.

He argues the real question is whether Alice Huang or her company, Megaspeed, was a Chinese asset, whether or not she was a trained spy. He cites China's National Intelligence Law, which requires citizens and organizations to cooperate with intelligence work. The Journal reports she was in contact with Chinese intelligence during the affair, though officials call the links circumstantial.

The host adds that Rubio oversaw a memo in March warning Trump that Huang might be compromised, though it did not say she was definitely a spy. Megaspeed was added to a trade blacklist on Monday after Treasury Secretary Bessent says Commerce under Howard Lutnik had blocked it for months. The Justice Department is investigating possible export violations, and Rubio walked away from a question on the matter.

The host notes that Chamath had said on Friday that no decision should be made at Nvidia until the congressional hearings were done, yet Huang is back before they have started. Huang is due to appear before House committees on December 1st and the Senate Banking Committee on December 3rd. Senators Kennedy and Cotton say the bigger question is China, and Cotton notes that bipartisan chip export legislation is coming. The House China committee also reports that American firms rely on Chinese open weight models and has written to companies including DoorDash and Airbnb.

The host calls the White House intervention risky. If chips reached China through lax oversight at Commerce, he says, Democrats will argue Trump saved a company that was too big to fail. He quotes Hakeem Jeffries, the Wall Street Journal editorial board, Wes Moore, Ro Khanna and Hillary Clinton, who calls it super gate. He warns of a time bomb that could include insider trading, and plays Jason Calacanis on why winning the AI race matters.

Zohran Mamdani ties the saga to pensions and concentrated wealth. The host says Democrats are now a two to one favorite for 2028 on Kalshi. He plays Eric Holder saying the next nominee must go back to confronting history and a DEI-infused agenda. The DNC plans twelve debates starting in June, with a pledge to denounce super PAC and dark money spending and with creators and influencers on stage. The host mocks the pledge, saying candidates can simply disavow ads, and notes unions spent over 200 million dollars in 2024.

Gavin Newsom's commutation of death row sentences is attacked after a report that at least 34 of the inmates were convicted in murders of law enforcement officers. The brother of a murdered detective speaks at the White House about his pain. Newsom also calls for reforming the presidential pardon power and accuses Trump of selling mercy. The host says the pardon power should largely go away, and points to Bill Clinton's pardons. Trump says there is no compromise on public safety, and Attorney General Blanche issued a memo directing prosecutors to seek the death penalty in heinous federal crimes and speed up executions.

The host then covers the controversy over lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Nearly five tons of it have re-crystallized and could explode on their own, so the Army wants a controlled detonation. Trump said he would wait for the Eighth Circuit and for Iowa's governor-elect Rob Sand to agree, and Sand was noncommittal. An appeals court cleared the way on Tuesday, and the acting Army secretary said every agency agreed. The Army predicts minimal soil contamination within 3,000 feet.

Last, the host turns to a Washington Post report that federal scientists see some evidence tying the weedkiller glyphosate, the main ingredient in Roundup, to cancer, particularly non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Animal studies found tumors in mice and rats. European regulators say the evidence does not meet the bar for calling it carcinogenic, while the international cancer agency disagrees. The host calls the evidence contradictory and says further study and limits on mass use may be wise, though he is divided because of the economic costs.
